text: Section one: Principle one. onChange sends every key into state. Let's begin with the smallest version, a greeting that follows each letter. Let's take the name box apart and look at one prop at a time. First, we keep only onChange and leave out value for now. When the page opens, the box is empty, and the greeting says only hello. That's what figure six shows, a browser window at localhost five one seven three with a box labeled Name, still empty, and under it, a single line that says Hello with nothing after it yet. The box hands each change to our code. This file is App.jsx inside the src folder. Line one imports useState from React. Line three starts the App component, and line four makes a piece of state called name with its setter setName. It starts as an empty string. Then inside the main tag, there's a label with the word Name and on line ten, the input. It has only one prop, onChange, and that's a small arrow. It takes e and calls setName with e.target.value. The note there says React calls this arrow on every key. And on line twelve, a paragraph says Hello, then name in curly braces. Now the user types J, and the greeting says, "Hello, J," then O, and it says, "Hello, Jo." After four keys, the page looks like this. In figure seven, it's the same page after the user types John. The box holds John, and right under it, the greeting reads, "Hello, John." It followed every letter. You met onChange at the start of the lecture. React understands it on every input, text area, and menu. React calls it each time the user changes the text in the box. That means on every single key, not only when the user leaves the box. Our arrow takes the text from e.target.value and saves it with setName. The new state makes React render the greeting again. Think of a student who calls out each letter to the teacher while writing a word on paper. The teacher hears every letter, not only the finished word. Now, the message box and its live count. Now we build the first part of our contact form, a heading, a message box, and the count under it. So this one is ContactForm.jsx in the components folder. After the import, line four makes our state message with setMessage starting as an empty string. Lines six to eight are a named handler, handleMessageChange. It takes the event, e, and calls setMessage with e.target.value. That's all it does. Then we return a section with a heading that says Contact Us and a form. Inside the form, a label with the word Message and on line sixteen, a textarea tag whose onChange is handleMessageChange. Again, React calls the handler on every key. And line eighteen is the count, a paragraph with message.length in curly braces, then a slash, then two hundred. The count uses .length, the number of characters in a string. When the page opens, message is empty, so the count shows zero. Figure eight is the first version of the Contact Us form, just as the page opens. There's the heading Contact Us, an empty message box, and below it, the count, zero out of two hundred. The user types, "Where is my parcel?" And the count moves with every letter. And figure nine shows the same form afterwards. The message box now holds, "Where is my parcel?" And the count under it has climbed to nineteen out of two hundred. The count changed after every single letter. So who tells our code about each letter? Here is what happens on every key in order. The user presses a key in the message box. The browser puts the letter into the box first. Only then does React call handleMessageChange, and it hands over the event object. E.target.value reads the whole text of the box, so the new letter is already inside. SetMessage saves that text in state, and React renders ContactForm again, and the count shows the new length. Here's something that trips people up. React's onChange and the browser's change event are not the same. If you have written plain JavaScript, this may surprise you. The browser has its own event called change, and it does not fire on every key. In plain JavaScript, there are two different events you can listen to on a text box. You can see both of them in Page.js, one per line. Line one tells messageBox to listen for change in quotes and logs e.target.value. That one runs only when the user leaves the box. Line two is almost the same, but it listens for input in quotes, and that one runs on every key. The browser's change event waits until the user is done with the box and clicks somewhere else. The browser's input event fires on every change. React's onChange behaves like the second line, the input event. So the two share a name, but they are not the same. The browser's change event waits for the user to leave the box. React's onChange fires on every key. React also accepts onInput, which does the same job. React code uses onChange by long habit, so this book uses it too.
